lead: Radar sends out a radio pulse and listens for the echo. The delay gives range; the antenna direction gives bearing. Ground radars use the echo itself, and also interrogate each aircraft's transponder, to build a traffic picture. ADS-B goes further: the aircraft broadcasts its own satellite position twice a second and anyone in range can receive it. A tracker fuses all these plots into one picture for the controller and the cockpit. The same principles run the weather radar, the radio altimeter and collision avoidance.
prereq: You need geometric concepts of navigation for range and bearing as lines of position. The displays that show the traffic picture are in Electronic displays: PFD, MFD, EADI and EHSI.

sections.h3: A pulse radar, block by block

blocks.text: Radar means radio detection and ranging. A transmitter makes a short burst of radio energy, an antenna radiates it, and the receiver waits for the echo. The delay gives range and the antenna angle gives bearing, a circle and a line of position, so one radar fixes an aircraft by itself.

blocks.where: R is slant range in metres, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light, and t is the echo delay in seconds measured from the transmitted pulse. The 2 appears because the pulse travels out and back.

items: The transmitter generates a pulse of width τ at peak power P<sub>t</sub>.
The duplexer connects the antenna to the transmitter, then switches it to the receiver so the strong pulse cannot burn the receiver out.
The antenna — a rotating dish or a fixed phased array — radiates the pulse and later collects the echo.
The receiver amplifies the weak echo, and a threshold decides whether it is a real target or noise.
The timer reads t, the computer computes R, and the antenna angle gives the bearing in degrees.
The display plots one blip at that range and bearing.

blocks.text: Echo power drops as the fourth power of range: double the distance and only one-sixteenth comes back. That is why radar powers are measured in kilowatts, and why detection range is the hardest number to improve.

sections.h3: The radar equation, resolution and ambiguity

blocks.text: R<sub>max</sub> = [ P<sub>t</sub> G² λ² σ ÷ ((4π)³ P<sub>min</sub>) ]<sup>1/4</sup>
blocks.where: R<sub>max</sub> is the maximum detection range in metres; P<sub>t</sub> is the transmitted peak power in watts; G is the antenna gain, a pure number; λ is the wavelength in metres; σ is the radar cross-section of the target in square metres, set by shape and material rather than physical size; P<sub>min</sub> is the weakest echo the receiver can detect, in watts.

blocks.text: Pulse width and pulse repetition frequency set two different limits, and they are the pair students mix up.
ΔR = c τ ÷ 2      and      R<sub>u</sub> = c ÷ (2 × PRF)
blocks.where: ΔR is the range resolution in metres and τ the pulse width in seconds; R<sub>u</sub> is the maximum unambiguous range in metres and PRF the pulse repetition frequency in hertz, that is, how many pulses leave the antenna each second.

blocks.text: A short pulse separates targets in range; a low PRF gives a long unambiguous range. You cannot have both cheaply, so air-surveillance radars switch between several PRFs and stitch the answers together.

blocks.where: f<sub>d</sub> is the Doppler shift in hertz, v<sub>r</sub> is the radial (closing) component of target speed in m/s, and λ is the wavelength in metres. The shift is a rise in frequency when the target closes. An aircraft flying across the beam has v<sub>r</sub> near zero and vanishes into clutter.

blocks.text: Primary surveillance radar (PSR) works on the skin echo. Metal reflects the pulse, so every aircraft in the beam appears whether its transponder works or not. PSR gives range and azimuth and nothing else — no identity, no height.
Secondary surveillance radar (SSR) is a conversation. The ground station interrogates at 1030 MHz and the transponder replies at 1090 MHz.

items: Mode A: identity only — the four-digit octal squawk the pilot sets.
Mode C: pressure altitude in 100 ft steps, sent along with the identity.
Mode S: a unique 24-bit aircraft address, so one aircraft can be selected and data-linked.

blocks.text: ADS-B — automatic dependent surveillance, broadcast — removes the interrogation. About twice a second the aircraft sends extended squitters on 1090 MHz: 112-bit messages that between them carry its GNSS position and altitude, its velocity, and its identity. Automatic because nobody asks; dependent because the position comes from the aircraft's own navigation system (5.6); broadcast because everyone in range receives it. ADS-B Out transmits. ADS-B In receives traffic and ground-uplinked radar tracks (TIS-B); on the UAT data link it also receives weather (FIS-B).

TCAS/ACAS is a separate cooperative system riding on the same transponders. It interrogates nearby aircraft directly and needs no ground station. TCAS II shows its resolution advisory as a commanded climb or descent rate on the flight director and vertical-speed indicator. The crew must respond within a few seconds; the autopilot is normally disconnected, not driven by the RA (see Autopilot and automatic flight control).

The radio (radar) altimeter is a frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar in the 4.2–4.4 GHz band. It sweeps its frequency up and down in a triangle and mixes the echo with what it is transmitting now; the echo left earlier, at a different frequency, so the mixer gives a beat frequency proportional to height. It reads height above the ground below from 0 to about 2500 ft and feeds TAWS (terrain awareness) and autoland.

Doppler navigation radar sends three or four narrow beams down and forward, back and to the sides (a Janus arrangement); the Doppler shift of each, fd = 2V cos γ ÷ λ with γ the angle between beam and velocity, gives ground speed and drift with no ground station. Weather radar, usually X-band near 9.3 GHz, paints rainfall in colours (green, yellow, red, magenta for heavier rain) from echo strength, and finds turbulence and windshear from the spread of Doppler shifts.
Mapping and multimode radar, mostly military, switches one set between ground mapping (sharpened by synthetic aperture processing), terrain following and air-to-air search.

figure.caption: Top, the pulse radar chain of the first worked example. Bottom, the radio altimeter of the second: the echo is a delayed copy of the triangular sweep, and the beat between them, 20.3 kHz at 500 ft, is proportional to height.

spec.aria: Top, a block diagram: transmitter to duplexer to antenna; echoes return through the duplexer to the receiver and a timer that computes range as c t over 2; the display shows range and antenna bearing. Example values: unambiguous range 150 kilometres, resolution 150 metres, Doppler 2.88 kilohertz. Bottom, a graph of frequency from 4250 to 4370 megahertz against time over 20 milliseconds: the transmitted triangle sweeps 100 megahertz at 100 hertz, a dashed echo is the same triangle shifted later, and an arrow between them marks the beat frequency, 20.3 kilohertz at 500 feet.

examples.question: An airport surveillance radar transmits at 2.8 GHz with PRF = 1000 Hz and a pulse width of 1 µs. (a) Find the maximum unambiguous range. (b) Find the range resolution. (c) Find the Doppler shift of an aircraft closing at 300 kt.
steps: f<sub>d</sub> = 2 v<sub>r</sub> ÷ λ = (2 × 154.3) ÷ 0.1071 = 2881 Hz ≈ 2.88 kHz, a rise in frequency because the target closes.
examples.answer: Unambiguous range 150 km, range resolution 150 m, Doppler shift about 2.88 kHz upward.

examples.question: A radio altimeter sweeps ΔF = 100 MHz in a triangle at f<sub>m</sub> = 100 Hz, so f<sub>b</sub> = 4 ΔF f<sub>m</sub> R ÷ c. (a) Find the beat frequency at 500 ft. (b) What height gives a 20 kHz beat?
steps: The beat is proportional to height: 133 Hz per metre here, so a counter on the beat frequency reads height directly.
examples.answer: 20.3 kHz at 500 ft; a 20 kHz beat means 150 m (492 ft).

traps: PRF sets the unambiguous range and pulse width sets the range resolution — never the other way round.
Both formulas carry a factor 2 for the round trip, c τ ÷ 2 and c ÷ (2 × PRF). Drop it and every answer halves or doubles.
ADS-B is a broadcast, not an interrogation; nothing is sent to the aircraft to prompt it. SSR is the system that asks.
SSR asks at 1030 MHz and hears the reply at 1090 MHz. Reversing the pair is the standard one-mark trap.
More power buys detection range (radar equation), not resolution. Resolution is bought with a shorter pulse.

quiz.q: What does the duplexer do in a pulse radar?
quiz.a: It switches the antenna between the transmitter and the receiver, so the high-power pulse never reaches the sensitive receiver.

quiz.q: At which frequencies does SSR interrogate and reply?
quiz.a: Ground interrogation at 1030 MHz, transponder reply at 1090 MHz.

quiz.q: Why can a primary radar detect an aircraft with its transponder switched off, and why can it not report that aircraft's altitude?
quiz.a: PSR uses the skin echo reflected from the metal airframe, which needs no cooperation. It measures only range and antenna azimuth, so no height is available; height comes from Mode C or ADS-B.

quiz.q: Explain each word of 'automatic dependent surveillance — broadcast'.
quiz.a: Automatic: transmits without interrogation. Dependent: the position comes from the aircraft's own GNSS/INS. Surveillance: it reports position and identity for traffic tracking. Broadcast: one transmission, every receiver in range uses it.

quiz.q: A target recedes at 200 kt from a radar transmitting at 2.8 GHz. Find the Doppler shift and its sign.
quiz.a: 200 kt = 102.9 m/s; λ = 0.1071 m; f<sub>d</sub> = 2 × 102.9 ÷ 0.1071 = 1921 Hz, and the received frequency falls because the target is moving away.

quiz.q: Two aircraft are only 100 m apart in range on a radar with 1 µs pulse width. What does the controller see, and what would you change?
quiz.a: ΔR = 150 m, so the two appear as one blip. Shorten the pulse below about 0.67 µs; 0.5 µs gives ΔR = 75 m and separates them. The cost is less energy per pulse, so either shorter detection range or wider receiver bandwidth and more noise.

beyond: Not for the exam. ADS-B Out is mandated in much of the world's controlled airspace, and space-based receivers now track aircraft over oceans where no ground radar reaches. Research runs on passive radar that uses existing broadcast signals instead of its own transmitter, on counter-drone detection, and on low-cost FMCW arrays for small airports. Search terms: 1090ES, Mode S address, FMCW radar, radar equation, TCAS II.
